modalities.name: Plain Sight Paddock
modalities.tagline: Watch a herd as it really is, with no stories added.
modalities.whatItIs: Plain Sight Paddock is a new concept for small groups who spend an hour at the edge of a field with a few calm horses, goats or sheep, simply watching what they do. A facilitator and the animals' handler set the pace and keep everyone at a safe distance. Nothing is imagined, interpreted or worked on: the practice is plain, present-tense seeing.
modalities.coreIdea: The Ideal Parent Figure Protocol builds caring figures in the imagination; this pushes animal-assisted therapy the opposite way, toward a real animal seen exactly as it is, here and now. The skill is noticing when you start adding a story, such as 'she looks lonely', and coming back to what you can actually see and hear.
modalities.whatYouDo: You stand or walk slowly along the fence with two or three other people for about 45 minutes, describing aloud only what is in front of you: an ear turning, a tail swishing, one animal moving away from another. When someone slips into guessing what an animal feels or means, the facilitator gently asks what they actually saw. The session ends with a few minutes of quiet watching and no discussion of the past.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who live much of the time inside their own heads, stories or worries and want an hour of plain looking. It might also appeal to anyone who likes animals but finds talking about themselves hard.
modalities.cautions: Horses and other livestock can kick, bite or bolt, so stay where the handler places you and never walk into the middle of a herd. Mention allergies or a fear of large animals before booking, and the animals should always be free to move away.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Plain Sight Paddock. A small group spends an hour at a field's edge watching horses or goats and describing only what they see, no guessing at feelings or backstories. For people who live in their heads. Untested, led by trained handlers.

modalities.name: Curry Comb Company
modalities.tagline: Pairs groom a calm horse, attention resting on brush and coat.
modalities.whatItIs: Curry Comb Company is a proposed practice in which two people groom a calm horse or donkey together, under the eye of a trained handler. Instead of turning inward to explore feelings, attention goes outward into the hands: the brush, the coat, the animal's warmth and its small responses.
modalities.coreIdea: IFS turns attention inward, toward parts and their history; this takes animal work further outward, into simple shared care in the present. When inner commentary starts up, you go back to the next brush stroke instead of following it.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a partner spend about 40 minutes grooming the same animal in a quiet stable, one on each side, working through brushing, combing the mane and wiping the face in a set order the handler shows you. You talk only as much as the task needs, and the handler watches the animal's comfort and tells you when to swap sides or stop. The session closes with both of you standing beside the animal for a few quiet breaths.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel crowded by their own thoughts and want a calm, hands-on task that pulls attention outward. It may also suit anyone who would like gentle company with another person without having to make conversation.
modalities.cautions: Horses can startle, step on feet or kick, so you only groom animals the handler knows well, keep clear of the area behind the hind legs and follow every instruction. Allergies to horse hair and stable dust are common, and the animal's comfort decides how long the session lasts.
modalities.tweet: What if grooming a horse were the whole practice? Curry Comb Company is a new idea: two people brush one calm horse for 40 minutes, attention on hands, coat and breathing, with a handler close by. For busy minds that want a quiet, useful task.

modalities.name: The Animal's Agenda
modalities.tagline: No goals, no homework: the animal decides where the session goes.
modalities.whatItIs: The Animal's Agenda is a new concept for an open session with a trained animal and a professional in which nobody sets an agenda except the animal. You do not try to change your thoughts or reach a goal; you wait, notice and respond when the animal chooses to come close.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT plans every session and aims at change. Pushed the other way, animal work drops the plan, the targets and the effort to change, and lets the animal's own choices set the pace.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit or stand for up to an hour in a quiet room or small arena with a professional and a calm dog or horse that is free to move around. If the animal approaches, you can stroke it, lean on the fence beside it or simply share the space; if it wanders off, you let it. There is no worksheet or homework, and the professional mainly keeps things safe and says little.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel worn out by plans, goals and self-improvement and want a session where nothing is expected of them. It could also work for anyone who wants to practice waiting and letting contact come to them.
modalities.cautions: A loose animal needs a trained handler, a safe space and the freedom to leave, and no one should be pushed into contact if they are frightened or allergic. Because it sets no goals, it is not a replacement for structured care when someone needs treatment for a mental health condition.
modalities.tweet: Imagine a session where the only agenda belongs to the animal. In The Animal's Agenda, you share a quiet space with a calm dog or horse and wait; contact happens only if it comes to you. For anyone tired of goals and self-improvement. 🐾

modalities.name: Silent Lead Rope
modalities.tagline: Lead a horse in silence, speaking only through posture and breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Silent Lead Rope is an untested idea for a nearly wordless session: you lead a calm horse through a simple course using only your posture, pace, breath and a loose rope. A professional and a horse handler guide every step with gestures rather than explanations.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT leans on words, metaphors and talk about values, so this version of animal work leaves language behind altogether. A horse tends to respond to clear, calm body signals rather than to what you say, which keeps attention in the body and the present moment.
modalities.whatYouDo: For about 45 minutes you walk a horse on a lead rope around an arena, asking it to start, stop, turn and pass through a gate, without speaking. The professional shows you each task with a gesture and steps in if anything becomes unsafe. At the end you have a few minutes to say one or two words about what you noticed, if you want to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find talking about feelings hard, or who are tired of explaining themselves, and would rather learn by doing. It may also suit anyone curious about how much they communicate without words.
modalities.cautions: Leading a horse carries real risks of being stepped on, pulled or kicked, so it needs a calm, well-trained horse, sturdy shoes and a handler within reach at all times. People with a strong fear of horses, or a condition that affects balance, should talk it through with the team before starting.
modalities.tweet: Concept: Silent Lead Rope. You lead a calm horse around an arena without a word, using only posture, pace and breath, while a handler walks beside you. For people who are tired of explaining themselves. New and untested. 🐴

modalities.name: Donkey Pace Walks
modalities.tagline: Walk a calm donkey at its pace, and stop when it stops.
modalities.whatItIs: Donkey Pace Walks is a new concept for slow walks with a calm donkey on a lead, along a quiet lane or field path, with a handler alongside. The donkey sets the speed, and when it stops to look or graze, you stop too.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy brings hidden emotional learnings vividly to the surface so they can be understood; this heads the other way, toward settling, with nothing to figure out. Matching your pace to an unhurried animal is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: You meet a handler and one or two donkeys at a farm or sanctuary and walk for about 40 minutes, holding a lead rope or walking beside someone who does. There is no topic to discuss: you watch the path, the donkey's ears and the landscape, and wait whenever it pauses. Afterward you help lead the donkeys back to their field and say goodbye.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel rushed, wound up or stuck in analyzing everything and want an hour that is slow by design. It might also appeal to anyone who likes animals and gentle walking but feels uneasy around big horses.
modalities.cautions: Donkeys are calm but strong and can kick or plant their feet, so a trained handler stays with each animal and routes stay quiet and away from traffic. Check the weather and footing, mention any allergies, and remember that the donkeys' comfort limits how often and how far they walk.
modalities.tweet: Ever wanted to go at someone else's pace for once? Donkey Pace Walks is a new idea: lead a calm donkey down a quiet lane and stop whenever it stops. Nothing to analyze, nowhere to hurry, a handler alongside. Untested, slow by design.

modalities.name: Where the Dog Settles
modalities.tagline: In a talking circle, whoever the dog settles beside may speak.
modalities.whatItIs: Where the Dog Settles is a proposed format for a small talking group of five to eight people, led by a professional, in which a calm therapy dog wanders the circle freely and whoever it settles beside is invited to speak. Passing is always allowed, so the dog's choice is an invitation rather than a demand.
modalities.coreIdea: TRE works through the body, alone and without words; moving away from it, this puts words, listening and other people at the center. The dog's wandering sets the order of speaking, which takes away the pressure of deciding to go first.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit in a circle for about an hour while the professional names a light theme, such as something that went well this week, and the dog moves around the room as it likes. When it lies down or leans beside you, you can speak for a minute or two, stroke it while you talk or simply say 'pass'. If the dog rests in the middle, the professional opens the floor to anyone, and the hour ends with a quiet round of goodbyes to the dog.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who would like to talk in a group but freeze when they have to decide when to speak. It could also suit anyone who opens up more easily with an animal nearby.
modalities.cautions: Ask about allergies and fear of dogs before anyone joins, and the handler should watch the dog for signs of stress, give it breaks and never steer it toward anyone. A group like this is a place to talk, not crisis care, so anyone in serious distress should also have individual support.
modalities.tweet: What if a calm dog decided who speaks next? Where the Dog Settles: a small talking circle where the dog wanders freely and whoever it lies beside may speak, or say 'pass'. A new idea for people who freeze at the thought of going first.

modalities.name: Reading Ears and Tails
modalities.tagline: Learn to read an animal's yes, no and maybe before touching.
modalities.whatItIs: Reading Ears and Tails is a new concept for a guided small-group course in reading animal body language, taught by a professional with calm dogs or horses. You learn to spot signs of comfort, worry and interest, and to ask an animal for contact and read its answer.
modalities.coreIdea: Focusing teaches patient attention to your own vague bodily sense of things; this turns the same patience outward, to another body's signals, with a professional guiding. Asking before touching, and respecting a no, is practiced as a real skill.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions with three or four others, you watch a calm animal while the professional points out ears, tail, eyes, weight shifts and yawns, and what each might mean. You then take turns offering a hand at a respectful distance and saying aloud whether you read a yes, a no or a maybe, and the handler confirms or corrects you. Over several weeks the animals and their signals become more varied.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to feel more confident and safe around animals, and anyone who wants to practice consent and boundaries in a concrete, low-stakes way. It could also interest people who find other people's moods hard to read.
modalities.cautions: Even calm animals can bite, scratch or kick when their signals are missed, so only work with trained animals and handlers and keep to the distances you are shown. Signals vary between animals and species, so what you learn is a guide rather than a certainty.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Reading Ears and Tails, a small-group course where a professional teaches you to read a dog's or horse's yes, no and maybe before you touch. Asking first, and respecting a no, becomes a real skill. For anyone nervous or curious around animals.

modalities.name: The Morning Feed Round
modalities.tagline: A fixed morning routine caring for real animals' real needs.
modalities.whatItIs: The Morning Feed Round is an invented practice in which you join a keeper at a farm or animal sanctuary and work through the same set morning routine on every visit: feeding, fresh water, checking each animal and cleaning. The animals depend on the job being done, which makes the practice concrete and practical rather than reflective.
modalities.coreIdea: Aletheia Coaching follows whatever unfolds inside you, with few fixed steps; going the other way, this is an outward, step-by-step task with a clear result. Being trusted with real needs, in the same order every time, is the heart of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week you arrive early, sign in and spend about two hours working through a checklist the keeper has written for your group of two or three people. You prepare feeds, refill water, check that each animal is eating and moving normally, clean out a stall and note what you did. The keeper goes over the checklist with you before you leave and adds one new task when you are ready.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel adrift and want a reliable routine with a visible purpose, for example during unemployment, after retirement or after a hard period. It may also suit anyone who would rather do something useful with their hands than talk.
modalities.cautions: Farm work involves lifting, slippery floors, tools and animals that can push, kick or bite, so the keeper should train and supervise you and give you only tasks that match your fitness. Wash your hands after animal contact, and mention allergies or health conditions beforehand.
modalities.tweet: Something new: The Morning Feed Round. Join a keeper at a farm or sanctuary for two hours and work the same checklist every visit: feed, water, check, clean, log. Real animals rely on it. For anyone who wants a routine with a visible point.

modalities.name: Hoofprint Team Course
modalities.tagline: A small team plans together to guide a horse through a course.
modalities.whatItIs: Hoofprint Team Course is a new concept for a structured group program in which teams of three or four guide a calm horse through a course of poles and cones, led by a professional and a handler. Each session has a set goal, a planning stage and a review, so the work stays practical and easy to review.
modalities.coreIdea: Do Nothing meditation drops every goal and lets go of control. Its opposite here is a clear task, a shared plan and deliberate change, done as a team, and since a horse cannot be talked into anything, the team finds out what actually works.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 90-minute session starts with a short briefing on the day's course, then your team has ten minutes to agree a plan without touching the horse. You carry out the plan with the handler beside you, swap roles and try again, and the professional leads a short review of what you planned against what happened. Over six to eight weeks the courses get harder and the planning time gets shorter.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to practice teamwork, clear communication or leadership in a concrete way, for example in a youth group, a work team or a recovery program. It could also work for anyone who learns better by doing than by discussing.
modalities.cautions: Several people moving around a horse raises the risk of kicks and knocks, so the handler controls every approach, marks clear safe zones and can stop the exercise at any time. Competitive pressure should stay low, and the horse gets regular breaks and short sessions.
modalities.tweet: Proposed: Hoofprint Team Course. Teams of three or four agree a plan, then guide a calm horse through poles and cones while a handler keeps everyone safe, and afterward compare the plan with what really happened. For people who learn teamwork by doing.

modalities.name: The Unearned Welcome
modalities.tagline: Let a friendly dog's welcome reach you without trying to earn it.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unearned Welcome is an untested idea for small-group visits with friendly, trained dogs, where the only task is to notice being greeted. Instead of producing kind feelings on purpose, you let real warmth arrive from a real animal and see what happens.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta builds goodwill by repeating phrases toward people you picture in your mind; this reverses the direction, toward receiving warmth that is really there, with no phrases and no effort. Being welcomed without having done anything to earn it is the core experience.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and four or five others sit on low chairs or cushions in a quiet room for about 45 minutes while a handler lets two or three friendly dogs come and greet each person in turn. You can stroke a dog, let it lean against you or just watch, and the professional invites you to notice whatever comes up, awkwardness included, without needing to say it. The session closes with a short round where anyone can share one moment that stood out.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to accept kindness, or who feel they must earn every bit of affection. It may also appeal to anyone who finds loving-kindness phrases forced and wants something more direct.
modalities.cautions: Being welcomed warmly can stir up unexpected sadness or old feelings of not being wanted, so the professional should be ready to slow things down and suggest further support. Ask about dog allergies and fears first, and the dogs should never be made to greet anyone.
modalities.tweet: For people who struggle to accept kindness, a new idea: The Unearned Welcome. Friendly trained dogs greet each person in a small group, and your only job is to notice being welcomed without earning it. A handler and a professional lead. Not yet tested.

modalities.name: One Animal, Many Weeks
modalities.tagline: Get to know one animal, week after week, in a small group.
modalities.whatItIs: One Animal, Many Weeks is a new concept for a ten-week program in which a small group visits the same animal, such as a sanctuary goat, pony or dog, at the same time each week. The point is a growing relationship: learning one animal's habits, likes and history, and letting it get to know you.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana watches each experience arise and pass, alone and in silence; this goes toward a relationship that continues and deepens over time, shared with others. Continuity, rather than a single moment, is what the practice builds.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you spend about an hour with your group and the same animal, guided by its handler: you notice what has changed, offer the care or play it enjoys and swap stories about it. The professional keeps a light thread running between sessions, such as what you learned last time and what you are curious about now. In the final week the group plans a proper goodbye, which is part of the practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find relationships hard to sustain, or who are rebuilding trust, and want a gentle, predictable bond to practice with. It might also appeal to anyone who would like a weekly fixed point that involves both people and an animal.
modalities.cautions: Endings can be hard, so the program should prepare for the goodbye from the start and point people to support if it brings up grief. The animal's welfare comes first: if it is unwell or stressed the session changes or stops, and allergies or fears should be raised before joining.
modalities.tweet: Same animal, same time, every week for ten weeks. One Animal, Many Weeks is a new concept: a small group visits one sanctuary goat or pony, learns its habits and ends with a proper goodbye. For people rebuilding trust.

modalities.name: Siesta Company
modalities.tagline: Rest or doze while a calm dog naps nearby; nothing is asked.
modalities.whatItIs: Siesta Company is a proposed practice of shared rest: a handler brings a calm dog to someone who is in bed or in a chair, at home, in hospital or in a care home, and the dog naps on its own blanket nearby while the person rests too. There is no task, no exercise and no need to talk or even to stroke the dog.
modalities.coreIdea: HIIT pushes the body to its limit in timed bursts; this goes as far the other way as it can, to complete stillness, calm and acceptance. Resting in company is the whole activity, not a gap between efforts.
modalities.whatYouDo: At a set rest time, such as early afternoon, the handler settles the dog on a blanket beside your bed or chair, dims the lights if you like and sits quietly nearby for about 30 minutes. You can doze, watch the dog sleep, rest a hand on it if it is close, or chat softly with the handler about anything, including animals you have known. The visit ends when you wake or the time is up, with no feedback and no plan for next time unless you want one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are ill, recovering, very tired or living with limited mobility, for whom most activities ask too much right now. It could also suit anyone who rests better with a calm presence nearby.
modalities.cautions: Hospitals and care homes need clear hygiene rules, and visits should be skipped for people with weakened immune systems, allergies or open wounds unless their care team agrees. The dog must be relaxed in that setting and free to leave, and the handler stays awake and in charge of the dog throughout.
modalities.tweet: For days when moving is too much: Siesta Company, a new concept. A handler brings a calm dog that naps on its blanket beside your bed or chair while you rest too. No task, no talking, not even petting required. Company for people who are ill or exhausted.

modalities.name: Pen and Paw Hour
modalities.tagline: Quiet writing time with a calm dog resting at your feet.
modalities.whatItIs: Pen and Paw Hour is a new concept for a still, private hour of reflective writing with a calm therapy dog resting at your feet and its handler, a trained professional, sitting quietly across the room. You write about whatever is on your mind, and afterward you decide whether to share any of it.
modalities.coreIdea: Team sport is loud, fast and full of other people; at the opposite pole, this is an almost private, still hour with a companion that asks for nothing. The dog's quiet presence is meant to keep the solitude from feeling lonely.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit at a table or in a soft chair in a small, quiet room for about an hour, with the dog lying beside you and a notebook in your lap. You write, pause to stroke the dog, look out of the window or simply rest, and the professional steps in only if you ask or if the dog needs a break. In the last ten minutes you can read a line aloud, talk about what came up or keep it all to yourself.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think best on paper but find writing alone heavy, including those working through something they are not ready to say out loud. It could also suit anyone who wants a calm, private hour with no social demands.
modalities.cautions: Writing about painful things can bring up strong feelings, so the professional should be trained to respond and to offer further help, especially if trauma or risk comes up. The usual checks for allergies, fear of dogs and the dog's own stress apply.
modalities.tweet: Some things are easier to write with a dog at your feet. Pen and Paw Hour is a new concept: an hour of quiet, private writing with a calm therapy dog resting beside you and a professional across the room. Share it afterward, or don't.

modalities.name: Ten-Minute Dog Break
modalities.tagline: A scheduled ten-minute pause with a therapy dog and your colleagues.
modalities.whatItIs: Ten-Minute Dog Break is a new concept for a short, scheduled pause at work or college: once a week, at a fixed time, a therapy dog team visits and small groups take ten minutes away from their desks. Each break follows the same short script, so it fits into a busy day without asking much of anyone.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance training is long, solitary and self-driven. This turns it around into a brief, guided stop shared with the people you work beside: a pause, not a project.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every week at the same time, a handler and a calm dog set up in a quiet room, and groups of two to five colleagues come in for ten minutes. The handler leads a simple routine: say hello to the dog, stroke it while taking three slow breaths, then each person says one sentence about how their week is going, if they want to, before saying goodbye. Then you go back to work.
modalities.whoItsFor: People in busy workplaces, schools or colleges who have no time for a full session but would welcome a short, friendly break with the people around them. It could also work for teams who rarely talk about anything but tasks.
modalities.cautions: The dog needs a calm room, a limit on the number of groups and quiet breaks, and colleagues with allergies or a fear of dogs should be able to skip it without explanation. A ten-minute break is not support for someone in crisis, who should be pointed to proper help.
modalities.tweet: Prototype idea: Ten-Minute Dog Break. Once a week a therapy dog team visits your workplace, and small groups get ten minutes: say hi, three slow breaths while stroking the dog, one sentence each about your week, back to work. For teams with no time to spare.

modalities.name: Featherweight Holding
modalities.tagline: Practice gentleness by holding a small, calm animal on your lap.
modalities.whatItIs: Featherweight Holding is an untested idea for small-group sessions in which each person gently holds a small, calm animal on a lap blanket, such as a guinea pig, a hen or a small dog used to handling, guided by a handler. The theme is gentleness: how lightly you can hold something alive and fragile, and how it feels to do so.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training moves heavy loads with effort and control; this explores the reverse, the lightest possible touch, stillness and letting go of control. The animal's comfort is the measure of how gentle you are being.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit with four or five others in a calm room for about 45 minutes while the handler shows each person how to support an animal on a blanket on their lap. You hold or stroke it as lightly as you can, and when the animal shows it wants to move, you let it go back to its pen. The professional invites quiet conversation about gentleness, including being gentle with yourself, and nobody has to speak.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are hard on themselves or always in control, and who want to practice softness in a very concrete way. It may also suit older adults or anyone with limited strength, since nothing heavy is involved.
modalities.cautions: Small animals are easily stressed or hurt, so only animals that tolerate handling take part, sessions are short, and the handler watches closely and stops if an animal seems uneasy. Mention allergies first, and wash your hands afterward to lower the risk of infection.
modalities.tweet: The opposite of lifting heavy: Featherweight Holding, a new concept where you hold a small, calm animal on your lap as gently as you possibly can, with a handler guiding. A practice in softness for people who are always hard on themselves.

modalities.name: Sanctuary Life Stories
modalities.tagline: Meet rescued animals and hear how each one came to be here.
modalities.whatItIs: Sanctuary Life Stories is a new concept for small-group visits to an animal sanctuary, where a keeper introduces rescued animals and tells each one's story, from how it arrived to how it has settled. You spend time with the animals and talk together about what their stories bring to mind.
modalities.coreIdea: Qigong works on your own body through a set, repeated form; this leans the other way, toward open-ended attention to another creature's life story, shared in conversation. Hearing how an animal arrived, adjusted and learned to trust again becomes a gentle way to think about your own story.
modalities.whatYouDo: You walk slowly around the sanctuary with a keeper and three to six others for about 90 minutes, stopping at a few animals, such as an elderly horse, a three-legged dog or a flock of rescued hens. At each stop the keeper tells the animal's story and you can stroke it where the keeper allows, or simply watch, then the group talks for a few minutes about what stood out. There is no set structure beyond the walk, and no one has to share anything personal.
modalities.whoItsFor: People going through change or recovery who find it easier to think about their own story through someone else's. It may also suit animal lovers who want a gentle, meaningful outing with others.
modalities.cautions: Animals with hard pasts can be unpredictable, so keepers decide which animals you meet and how close you get, and some stories may be upsetting to hear. Mention allergies first, wear sturdy shoes and wash your hands after touching animals.
modalities.tweet: Concept sketch: Sanctuary Life Stories. A keeper walks a small group around an animal sanctuary and tells how each rescued animal arrived and settled in. You spend time with them and talk about what their stories stir up. For people facing big changes.

modalities.name: Head to Tail, Slowly
modalities.tagline: A fixed, wordless sequence of slow strokes, alone with one calm dog.
modalities.whatItIs: Head to Tail, Slowly is an invented practice for quiet one-to-one sessions in which you stroke a calm dog that enjoys touch in the same slow sequence every time, from the head along the back to the tail. There is no conversation, and a handler stays in the room but out of the way.
modalities.coreIdea: Socializing fills time with talk and many people. This version of animal work offers the opposite kind of company: one animal, no words and a fixed ritual of touch, done the same way each time.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each 30-minute session follows the same steps: you sit on the floor or a low chair, let the dog sniff your hand, then work through a set series of long, slow strokes along its head, neck, back and sides, pausing every few strokes with your hand still. In each pause you wait to see whether the dog leans in for more or moves away, and you carry on only if it leans in. The handler ends the session with a quiet signal, and you leave without needing to talk about it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel drained by social life, or overwhelmed by noise and talk, and want a calm, predictable session with no social demands. It may also suit anyone who settles more easily with an animal than with people.
modalities.cautions: Only dogs that clearly enjoy being handled take part, sessions stay short, and the handler stops at the first sign of discomfort, such as lip-licking, turning away or stiffening. Mention allergies or fear of dogs first, and avoid any area the handler says the dog dislikes being touched.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: a quiet room, one calm dog and the same slow strokes from head to tail, pausing to check it still wants more. Head to Tail, Slowly is a new idea with no talking at all. For anyone worn out by people and noise. 🐕

modalities.name: Eight Lessons, One Dog
modalities.tagline: An eight-week indoor course practicing relationship basics with a dog.
modalities.whatItIs: Eight Lessons, One Dog is a new concept for an eight-week indoor course in which a professional uses one well-trained dog to practice the basics of relationships, one theme per week. The themes are greeting, asking clearly, waiting, saying no, trust, repair after a mistake, play and saying goodbye.
modalities.coreIdea: Nature walks are open, outdoors and self-led; this brings animal work indoors, with a clear structure and a trained guide. Each week's small, concrete exercise with the dog gives a theme from human relationships something real to practice on.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a group of three to five, you meet weekly for an hour in the same room, with the same dog and the same professional. Each session has a set shape: a greeting ritual with the dog, a short exercise on the week's theme, such as asking the dog to wait or noticing when it says no, a conversation about how the theme shows up in your own life, and a closing goodbye. The last session marks the end of the course and of the group's time with the dog.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a gentle, structured way to practice relationship skills, such as asking for what they need or handling goodbyes. It could also work for those who cannot easily get outdoors or who prefer a predictable indoor setting.
modalities.cautions: Themes like saying no, trust and goodbyes can touch old relationship pain, so the course should be led by a qualified professional who can offer more support. The dog needs breaks, a calm room and a handler watching for stress, and people with allergies or fear of dogs should say so first.
modalities.tweet: Eight weeks, one dog, eight themes: greeting, asking, waiting, saying no, trust, repair, play, goodbye. Eight Lessons, One Dog is a new concept: practice each one with a calm dog indoors, then talk about where it shows up with people.

modalities.name: Lost Companion Walks
modalities.tagline: Small group walks with therapy dogs for people grieving a pet.
modalities.whatItIs: Lost Companion Walks is a proposed format for small, professionally led group walks for people who have lost a pet, with one or two calm therapy dogs along. You walk, take turns holding a lead if you want to, and talk with others who understand that this kind of grief is real.
modalities.coreIdea: Sensory mindfulness keeps quiet, solitary attention on present sensation; this goes toward company, conversation and memory, shared on the move. Walking beside a living dog can make it easier to talk about one who has died, without having to sit face to face.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for six weeks, four to eight people meet a professional and a handler with one or two calm dogs for a 45-minute walk on a quiet, level route. Along the way you can share stories about the animal you lost, walk a stretch holding a dog's lead or simply listen, and the professional offers one gentle prompt each week, such as a favorite memory or a habit you miss. The walk ends with a few minutes of quiet together before people head home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People grieving a pet who feel that friends and family do not quite understand the loss. It could also suit people who stopped going out after losing a dog and want a gentle way back outdoors.
modalities.cautions: Being around dogs can bring grief to the surface, so anyone can walk without a dog, step away or leave early, and the professional should point people whose grief stays overwhelming toward further support. The usual checks for allergies, fear of dogs, weather, footing and the dogs' welfare apply.
modalities.tweet: Grieving a pet can be lonely. Lost Companion Walks is a new idea: a small weekly walk with calm therapy dogs and a professional, sharing stories of the animals you lost, or just walking. For people whose friends don't quite get it.

modalities.name: Hay and Hoof Listening
modalities.tagline: Sit quietly in a stable and listen to the animals, not music.
modalities.whatItIs: Hay and Hoof Listening is a new concept for guided listening sessions in a barn or stable at feeding time, where you sit and listen to the animals instead of to music. Chewing, breathing, shifting hooves and soft calls become the only soundtrack.
modalities.coreIdea: Music shapes sound to carry emotion and expression; here the sound is unarranged and alive, and you only receive it. A guide gives the listening a simple shape, but nothing is performed or expressed.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a few others sit on hay bales or chairs in a stable for about 40 minutes while a guide leads a short listening sequence: sounds close by, sounds further away, then the quiet between them. Afterward you can walk slowly along the stalls with the handler, greet the animals and say a few words about what you heard. Phones stay off and no music is played.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find silence uncomfortable but music too emotionally loaded, and want something calm and real to listen to. It could also interest anyone who enjoys the atmosphere of barns and stables.
modalities.cautions: Stables can be dusty and full of allergens, so people with asthma or allergies should check first, and you stay where the handler places you, out of reach of hooves. The animals' routine comes first, so the group stays quiet and keeps a respectful distance at feeding time.
modalities.tweet: Ever listened to a stable at feeding time? Hay and Hoof Listening is a new idea: sit on a hay bale for 40 minutes and listen to chewing, breathing and hooves as a guide leads you from near sounds to far ones. No music, no phones, just the barn.

modalities.name: Only What You Feel
modalities.tagline: A simple movement routine with no visualizing, just real sensation.
modalities.whatItIs: Only What You Feel is a new concept for a short, fixed movement routine that you teach yourself from a one-page card and practice with no imagery at all. Many mind-body practices ask you to picture energy, light or flowing water; here you attend only to sensations you can actually feel, such as weight, stretch, warmth and air on the skin.
modalities.coreIdea: The Ideal Parent Figure Protocol is therapist-led, rich in imagined scenes and reaches far into the past; this pushes qigong the other way, to a self-led, purely physical routine anchored in the present. If an image or memory appears, you let it go and return to what the body is sensing.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing in any quiet spot, indoors or out, you work through eight slow movements, such as raising the arms, turning at the waist and shifting weight from foot to foot, for about 20 minutes. At each movement you silently name one real sensation, like heaviness in the hands or a stretch along one side. You do it alone, daily if you like, with no teacher, music or recording.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find visualization frustrating or unsettling, or who want a body practice with nothing to imagine and nothing to believe. It may also suit anyone who wants a simple routine they can start alone today.
modalities.cautions: Move within a comfortable range, sit down or adapt any movement that strains your joints or balance, and keep up any treatment you already have. If strong memories or unusual sensations keep coming up, pause and talk to a doctor or an experienced teacher.
modalities.tweet: No visualizing energy, no picturing light. Only What You Feel is a new concept: a 20-minute standing routine you teach yourself from one card, noticing only real sensations like weight, stretch and warmth. For anyone who finds imagery exercises frustrating.

modalities.name: The Hundred Rises
modalities.tagline: One slow arm raise, repeated a hundred times with the breath.
modalities.whatItIs: The Hundred Rises is an untested idea for a practice made of a single movement: you raise the arms slowly on an in-breath and lower them on an out-breath, one hundred times. It is as simple and repetitive as a practice can be, and after one short demonstration it can be done alone anywhere.
modalities.coreIdea: IFS explores many inner voices and their histories with a therapist; this pares qigong down to one movement, one rhythm and one point of attention, done on your own. Total repetition leaves nothing to choose, analyze or negotiate.
modalities.whatYouDo: You stand with your feet hip-width apart and count each rise silently from one to one hundred, which takes roughly 10 to 20 minutes, depending on your natural breathing pace. If you lose count, you carry on from the last number you remember rather than starting again. Done daily, it becomes a fixed ritual with a clear beginning and end.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds feel crowded with competing voices and who want something utterly simple and slow to do. It might also appeal to those who like counting and clear endpoints.
modalities.cautions: Shoulder or neck problems may call for a smaller range or fewer repetitions, and breathing should stay easy and natural, never forced, so stop if you feel dizzy. Anyone with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before taking up a repetitive meditative practice.
modalities.tweet: One movement, one hundred times. The Hundred Rises is a new idea: raise your arms on the in-breath, lower them on the out-breath, and count to a hundred. Ten to twenty minutes, nothing to decide. For minds that feel crowded.

modalities.name: Before-Bed Sway
modalities.tagline: A slow, goal-free movement routine for the last minutes before bed.
modalities.whatItIs: Before-Bed Sway is a new concept for a gentle, fixed movement routine done in dim light just before bed, with no goal to reach and nothing to get right. The movements are slow swaying, loose arm swings and soft knee bends, followed by standing still for a few breaths.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT tests and changes thoughts. Pushed away from it, qigong becomes all body and no argument: thoughts that come up are neither disputed nor followed, attention returns to the feet, and nothing is meant to improve.
modalities.whatYouDo: With the lights low and screens off, you stand in your bedroom and follow the same short sequence for about 15 minutes: sway from side to side, swing the arms loosely, bend the knees softly, then stand still and breathe. If you notice yourself trying hard to relax properly, you let that effort go as well. Then you go straight to bed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who lie awake with racing thoughts and find that thinking-based techniques make them more alert. It may also suit anyone who wants a short, wordless ritual to end the day.
modalities.cautions: Move slowly and keep a hand near a wall or the bed if you feel unsteady in dim light. Ongoing sleep problems can have medical causes, so talk to a doctor if poor sleep lasts more than a few weeks.
modalities.tweet: A thought experiment for restless nights: Before-Bed Sway. Lights low, screens off, 15 minutes of slow swaying, loose arm swings and soft knee bends, then bed. No goal and no getting it right. For people whose thoughts speed up when they try to relax.

modalities.name: Toes to Crown
modalities.tagline: Every joint moved in order, from the toes up to the crown.
modalities.whatItIs: Toes to Crown is an invented routine, a completely fixed sequence that moves every joint in the body in order, from the toes up to the neck, with a set number of slow circles for each. It is learned once from a teacher or a printed chart and then practiced alone, exactly the same every time.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT is flexible, conversational and full of metaphor; at the other extreme sits a literal, wordless, fully mapped routine. Knowing exactly what comes next is part of the appeal.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing, or seated if you need to, you make eight slow circles with each joint in turn (toes, ankles, knees, hips, spine, shoulders, elbows, wrists, fingers and neck), breathing slowly throughout. A full round takes about 25 minutes. You always finish by standing still for one minute before moving on with your day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like order and predictability and want a thorough daily routine they never have to think about. It may also suit those whose minds get busy when instructions are vague.
modalities.cautions: Make small, pain-free circles, shrink or skip any joint that is injured or arthritic, and use the seated version if your balance is unsteady. Keep neck circles slow and partial, and check with a doctor or physiotherapist first if you have a neck or spine condition.
modalities.tweet: Proposal: Toes to Crown, a fixed routine that moves every joint in order, toes up to neck, eight slow circles each, about 25 minutes. The same every day, nothing to decide. For people who like knowing exactly what comes next.

modalities.name: One Move a Minute
modalities.tagline: Movements slowed down until each one takes a full minute.
modalities.whatItIs: One Move a Minute is a new concept for an extremely slow movement practice: you take a short, fixed sequence of simple movements and slow each one down until it lasts a whole minute. At that speed there is little to do except feel the movement happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy brings strong, hidden emotional learnings to the surface to find the meaning in them; this heads toward deep settling, with no meaning to find. Slowness itself is the method.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a timer or a clock in view, you spend about 20 minutes on a sequence of five movements, such as raising one arm, turning the head, shifting your weight and bending the knees slightly, each stretched across sixty seconds and repeated. You practice alone, standing in a quiet place, and if you speed up you simply slow down again. The sequence takes a few minutes to learn and can then be practiced on your own.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel constantly hurried or keyed up and want a practice built entirely on slowing down. It could also work for those who find emotion-focused work overwhelming and want something purely physical.
modalities.cautions: Moving this slowly can tire the legs and test balance, so keep movements small and stand near a wall or chair. People with a history of psychosis or another serious mental illness should get medical advice before starting intensive meditative movement.
modalities.tweet: What if each movement took a full minute? One Move a Minute: five simple moves, each slowed to sixty seconds, about 20 minutes in all, alone and in silence. An untested practice for anyone who feels permanently hurried.

modalities.name: The Full Bowl
modalities.tagline: Move as smoothly as if carrying a brimming bowl.
modalities.whatItIs: The Full Bowl is a proposed movement form in which you move smoothly and steadily, as if carrying a bowl filled to the brim with water. Every movement is continuous, with no jerks, pauses or trembling, and the bowl sets the standard for smoothness.
modalities.coreIdea: TRE invites the body to shake and tremble on its own; this takes qigong the opposite way, toward deliberate smoothness, control and calm. Steady, unbroken motion is the whole aim.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the form in a few classes, you practice at home for about 20 minutes: you hold your hands as if cupping a bowl and move them through slow lifts, turns and circles while stepping gently, keeping everything level. Some people start with a real plastic bowl of water to feel the standard, then carry on with an imagined one. A teacher or practice partner can check your smoothness from time to time.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel jittery or shaky under stress and want to practice the opposite: smooth, deliberate movement. It may also suit those who like a clear standard to aim for.
modalities.cautions: Keep the knees soft and the steps small to protect your balance, and use a dry, clear floor if you practice with real water. If you have a tremor from a medical condition, adapt the form freely and take smoothness as a direction rather than a test.
modalities.tweet: New idea: The Full Bowl. You move through slow lifts and turns as if carrying a bowl filled to the brim, so nothing jerks or wobbles. A smooth, steady form for people who feel jittery under stress. Untested, about 20 minutes a day.

modalities.name: Mirror and Plumb Line
modalities.tagline: A precise form practiced at a mirror, correcting alignment each time.
modalities.whatItIs: Mirror and Plumb Line is a new concept for practicing a precise movement form in front of a full-length mirror with a vertical line marked down it, checking and correcting your alignment as you go. The aim is exactness: each posture should match the reference a teacher showed you.
modalities.coreIdea: Focusing waits patiently for a vague inner felt sense to form; this replaces the waiting with outward checking against a precise standard and active correction. You use your eyes and a fixed reference line to shape the body step by step.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher first shows you a short form and photographs or marks its key postures. At home you practice in front of a mirror with a strip of tape running down it, pausing at each key posture to line up your head, spine and hips with the tape and adjust, for about 25 minutes. Every few weeks the teacher checks your form and adds a finer detail.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy precision and visible progress and find open, inward practices too vague. It could also interest anyone who wants to work deliberately on posture.
modalities.cautions: Aim for comfortable alignment rather than forcing joints into perfect lines, especially with back, hip or knee problems. If checking the mirror feeds self-criticism about your body, cover it and work by feel for a while.
modalities.tweet: For people who like precision: Mirror and Plumb Line, a new concept where you practice a slow form at a mirror with a strip of tape down the middle, lining up head, spine and hips at each posture. Careful correction is the practice.

modalities.name: Twelve-Week Logbook
modalities.tagline: A self-led movement plan that grows weekly, tracked in a notebook.
modalities.whatItIs: Twelve-Week Logbook is an untested idea for a self-led, progressive movement program: you follow a written twelve-week plan that adds a little time or one new movement each week, and record every session in a notebook. Progress is planned, measured and visible on the page.
modalities.coreIdea: Aletheia Coaching lets things unfold in open conversation with a coach; this goes toward a written plan, steady progression and self-direction. The logbook turns a gentle practice into a clear training project.
modalities.whatYouDo: In week one you practice three simple movements for ten minutes a day, and each week the plan adds a few minutes or a new movement, until by week twelve you do a 30-minute form of eight movements. After each session you write the date, the length and one line about how your body felt. Every four weeks you read back through the log and adjust the plan if needed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are motivated by goals and tracking and want a gentle practice that still feels like progress. It may also suit anyone who has tried meditation but missed having a plan.
modalities.cautions: Progress at the pace of your body rather than the plan, and repeat a week or go back a step if anything hurts or you feel unwell. Keep up any treatment you already have, and talk to a doctor first if you have a heart, joint or balance condition.
modalities.tweet: Like a training plan, but slow: Twelve-Week Logbook is a new idea where a written plan adds a few minutes or one new movement each week, from 10 minutes up to a 30-minute form, and you log every session. For goal-driven people who want gentle progress.

modalities.name: Steady on One Leg
modalities.tagline: A small class that builds balance with slow, graded one-leg postures.
modalities.whatItIs: Steady on One Leg is a new concept for a small weekly class built around slow movements that challenge balance, from shifting weight to holding one-leg postures, arranged in graded levels. It has one clear aim, steadier balance, and every session follows the same structure.
modalities.coreIdea: Do Nothing meditation drops every aim and lets go of control; in the opposite direction, qigong gains a deliberate goal, graded steps and a teacher who coaches change. Working safely at the edge of your balance gives each session its focus.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a group of six to eight with a teacher, you spend about 45 minutes working through set levels: shifting weight, stepping slowly, lifting one heel, then holding one-leg postures while moving the arms. Everyone works at their own level beside a chair or wall, and the teacher moves you up a level once you are steady. Between classes you practice your current level for ten minutes a day at home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a gentle practice with a concrete physical goal, including older adults who would like to feel steadier on their feet. It might also appeal to anyone who likes being coached through clear levels.
modalities.cautions: Always practice beside a sturdy chair or wall on a non-slip floor, and move up a level only when the current one feels secure. People with a history of falls, dizziness or a balance disorder should check with a doctor or physiotherapist first.
modalities.tweet: Want to feel steadier on your feet? Steady on One Leg is a new concept: a small weekly class of slow balance movements in graded levels, from shifting weight to one-leg holds, always beside a chair, plus ten minutes of home practice a day.

modalities.name: Many Bodies, One Breath
modalities.tagline: A group moves in exact unison, timed to one shared breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Many Bodies, One Breath is a proposed group practice in which everyone moves through the same slow form in exact unison, timed to a leader's audible breathing. You can see and hear the people around you, and keeping together is the practice.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta sits alone and wishes well to people held in mind; this goes toward real people beside you, sensed directly through shared movement rather than phrases. Connection is felt in the body, not called up in the imagination.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twenty people stand in rows or a circle in a hall or park for about 30 minutes while a leader breathes slowly and audibly and moves through a simple form. Everyone matches the leader's breath and timing, glancing at their neighbors to stay together, without talking. At the end the group stands still for a minute before leaving.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel cut off and want a sense of belonging that does not depend on conversation. It may also suit those who find loving-kindness phrases abstract and want something more physical.
modalities.cautions: Breathe at your own comfortable pace if the leader's rhythm feels too slow, rather than holding your breath to keep up. Adapt any movement that strains your joints or balance, and anyone with a history of psychosis should get medical advice first.
modalities.tweet: Imagine twenty people in a park at dawn, moving as one, timed to a single leader's breath. Many Bodies, One Breath is a new concept for belonging without conversation: thirty minutes, no talking, just keeping together. 🌅

modalities.name: Measured Step Walking
modalities.tagline: A slow walking form that deliberately reshapes how you walk.
modalities.whatItIs: Measured Step Walking is a new concept for a slow walking form with set arm movements, practiced in a small group once a week and alone in between. Each step is placed deliberately, with the aim of a more upright, balanced and unhurried way of walking.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana sits still and observes sensation without trying to change it; this moves qigong into steady walking with a goal: changing how you carry yourself. Walking becomes something you train on purpose rather than something you only watch.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a teacher and a few others, you walk a set route around a hall or a park path for about 30 minutes, rolling each foot from heel to toe, swinging the arms in time and breathing with the steps. The teacher gives one cue at a time, such as lengthening the spine or softening the knees. Between classes you practice the walk for ten minutes a day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who would rather meditate while moving than sit still, and who want to work on posture or walking with a clear aim. It may also suit those who like a little company in their practice.
modalities.cautions: Choose level, safe ground, wear supportive shoes and slow down further if you feel unsteady. People with foot, knee or hip problems, or a balance condition, should adapt the steps and check with a doctor or physiotherapist.
modalities.tweet: Rather move than sit still? Measured Step Walking is a new concept: a slow walking form where you roll each foot heel to toe, swing your arms in time and breathe with your steps, with a teacher and a few others. About 30 minutes, once a week.

modalities.name: Minimum Muscle Practice
modalities.tagline: Gentle seated or lying movements using the least effort possible.
modalities.whatItIs: Minimum Muscle Practice is an untested idea for a seated or lying form in which every movement is done with the least muscle effort possible. It is designed for low-energy days, when even gentle standing exercise feels like too much.
modalities.coreIdea: HIIT drives effort and heart rate to the limit; this is qigong taken as far the other way as it goes, to almost no effort, deep calm and acceptance of the energy you have. The skill is finding out how little it takes to move.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting in a supported chair or lying on a bed, you follow a short fixed sequence of tiny movements, such as letting the hands float up a little, rolling the head slightly and spreading the fingers, for 10 to 15 minutes. With each one you notice which muscles you could let go of and still make the movement. A teacher shows you once, and after that you can practice alone with a short recording.
modalities.whoItsFor: People living with fatigue, chronic illness or a long recovery, for whom most exercise is out of reach for now. It could also work for anyone who tends to overdo things and wants to learn the opposite.
modalities.cautions: If fatigue is new, severe or unexplained, see a doctor before assuming it just needs rest. Keep up any treatment you already have, and stop if any movement causes pain or dizziness.
modalities.tweet: For low-energy days, a new idea: Minimum Muscle Practice. Sitting or lying down, you make tiny movements for 10 to 15 minutes and notice how little effort each one really needs. The opposite of high-intensity training, and that is the point.

modalities.name: Statue Minutes
modalities.tagline: Stand completely still, alone, letting every itch and urge pass.
modalities.whatItIs: Statue Minutes is a new concept for a solitary standing practice in which you hold one simple posture completely still for a set time, without reacting to itches, sounds or the urge to fidget. You start with a few minutes and build up slowly over weeks, using a posture a teacher has checked for you.
modalities.coreIdea: Team sport is fast, crowded and all about reacting to what others do; this is its opposite, with no one to react to and nothing to react with. Noticing an urge to move and letting it pass, again and again, is the skill being trained.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone in a quiet room, you take the standing posture a teacher showed you, with soft knees, arms resting in a gentle curve and eyes half open, and set a timer for five minutes at first. When an itch, a sound or a restless thought pulls at you, you notice it and stay still, and over the weeks you add a minute at a time up to about 20. Once a month the teacher checks your posture so that stillness does not turn into strain.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel driven to react to every message, noise or demand and want to practice the opposite in a simple, physical way. It could also suit anyone who likes a clear, measurable goal in a calm practice.
modalities.cautions: Standing still for a long time can make some people light-headed or stiff, so keep the knees soft, breathe normally, and move or sit down at once if you feel faint or anything hurts. People with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before taking up long, still meditative practice.
modalities.tweet: Itchy nose? Stay still anyway. Statue Minutes is a new idea: stand alone in one simple posture and let every itch, sound and urge to fidget pass, starting at five minutes and building to twenty. For people who react to everything.

modalities.name: Kettle Boil Breaks
modalities.tagline: Two-minute fixed movement breaks, tied to everyday moments like the kettle.
modalities.whatItIs: Kettle Boil Breaks is an invented practice made of very short, fixed movement routines of about two minutes, tied to moments that already happen through the day, such as waiting for the kettle, the printer or a page to load. Instead of one long session, you get many tiny ones.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance training means long, continuous effort. Turned around, practice becomes many brief, still and calm moments spread across the day, with each existing pause as the cue for the same short routine.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher shows you one two-minute routine, such as three slow arm raises, a gentle twist each way and a few breaths with your hands resting on your belly. You then do it each time a chosen cue comes up, perhaps six to ten times a day, standing wherever you are. Once a month you can go back to the teacher, alone or with a small group, to check the routine.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who never find time for a full session but have plenty of small waits in their day. It could also work for desk workers who sit for long stretches.
modalities.cautions: Keep the movements small enough for wherever you are, and skip them on slippery floors or in crowded spaces. It is gentle, but stop any movement that causes pain, and keep up any treatment you already have.
modalities.tweet: Waiting for the kettle? That is your practice. Kettle Boil Breaks is a new idea: one two-minute routine of slow arm raises, gentle twists and a few breaths, repeated whenever an everyday pause comes up. For people who never have time for a full session. ☕

modalities.name: Gravity Does the Work
modalities.tagline: Let your arms hang, swing and drop, with gravity doing the work.
modalities.whatItIs: Gravity Does the Work is a new concept for a relaxed movement form in which you let parts of the body hang, swing and settle under their own weight instead of lifting them with effort. Arms swing loosely from turning hips, shoulders drop, and the upper body hangs forward a little before slowly uncurling.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training works against gravity with effort, load and control; this lets gravity move the body while you do as little as possible. Letting go of control is the skill being practiced.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing with soft knees, you work through a fixed 15-minute sequence: loose arm swings driven by gentle turns of the hips, shoulders lifted and allowed to drop, wrists shaken loose and a slow, partial roll down and back up. You learn it in one or two classes and then practice alone, perhaps at the end of a stressful day. In each move the aim is to notice where you are still holding on and let it go.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry tension in their shoulders, jaw or back and find it hard to let go, including those used to pushing hard in the gym. It may also suit anyone who wants a very low-effort way to move.
modalities.cautions: Keep swings small and controlled enough not to jar the shoulders or back, and skip the roll down if you have back problems, low blood pressure or dizziness. Stop any movement that causes pain, and keep up any treatment you already have.
modalities.tweet: Strength training fights gravity. What if a practice let gravity win? Gravity Does the Work is a new concept: 15 minutes of loose arm swings, dropped shoulders and slow roll-downs, doing as little as possible. For people who never quite let go.

modalities.name: Write Your Own Form
modalities.tagline: Design your own fixed sequence of simple movements, then keep it.
modalities.whatItIs: Write Your Own Form is a proposed practice in which you build your own short movement sequence from a small menu of simple moves, write it down and then practice it unchanged, alone, every day. You are the author, the teacher and the student.
modalities.coreIdea: Animal-assisted therapy relies on a professional, a living partner and a relationship; this goes toward complete self-reliance, solitude and a structure you design yourself. Writing the form down and then sticking to it is the heart of the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: From a printed menu of about twenty basic moves, such as arm raises, side bends, slow turns and weight shifts, you choose six to eight, put them in an order and decide on the counts and breathing for each. You write the sequence on a card and practice it alone for 15 to 20 minutes a day for at least a month before changing anything. Some people add a simple image to each move, such as pushing a cloud or lifting water.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer to work things out for themselves and like owning their routine, including those who do not get on with classes or teachers. It may also suit anyone who has tried set forms and wants one that fits their own body.
modalities.cautions: Choose moves that suit your body and leave out anything that hurts, and if you have joint, heart or balance problems ask a physiotherapist to look over your sequence. Practicing alone means no one checks on you, so stop and seek medical advice if you notice unusual mental or bodily reactions.
modalities.tweet: Design your own practice, then stick to it. Write Your Own Form is a new idea: pick six to eight simple moves from a menu, write them on a card and practice them unchanged, alone, every day for a month. For people who do not get on with classes.

modalities.name: One-Hour Hermitage
modalities.tagline: One weekly hour of slow form practice in complete solitude.
modalities.whatItIs: One-Hour Hermitage is a new concept for one fully solitary hour a week of slow, fixed movement practice, with the phone off, the door closed and no contact with anyone. It is a planned retreat from social life, built around a form learned from a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Socializing fills time with people, talk and spontaneity; this pushes qigong the opposite way, into deliberate solitude, silence and a fixed routine. Being entirely alone on purpose, for a set time, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you go to a quiet room or a secluded outdoor spot, switch off your phone and follow a set plan for 60 minutes: ten minutes of still standing, a slow form repeated three times, then ten more minutes of still standing. You do not speak, read or listen to anything during the hour. A teacher gives you the form and the plan and checks in with you every couple of months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are surrounded by others all day, such as parents, carers or people in busy jobs, and rarely get a moment alone. It might also appeal to introverts who want a regular, protected time to recharge.
modalities.cautions: Solitude is restful for some people and hard for others, so if being alone brings up loneliness or low mood, shorten the hour and talk to someone about it. Keep a switched-off phone within reach for emergencies, and people with a history of psychosis should get medical advice before long solitary practice.
modalities.tweet: One hour a week, entirely alone, on purpose. One-Hour Hermitage is a new concept: phone off, door shut, a slow movement form and still standing for sixty minutes, with no talking and nothing to listen to. For parents, carers and anyone who is never alone.

modalities.name: Eyes Closed Indoors
modalities.tagline: A short indoor form practiced with eyes closed, steadied by inner sensing.
modalities.whatItIs: Eyes Closed Indoors is an untested idea for practicing a short, fixed movement form indoors with your eyes closed, relying on your inner sense of where your body is rather than on what you see. It is taught by a teacher and then practiced at home, in a small cleared space next to a wall.
modalities.coreIdea: Nature walks are open, outdoors and full of sights and sounds; this takes qigong into a closed room, with closed eyes and a fixed form. Turning vision off is meant to train your inner sense of position and balance, step by step.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn a simple five-movement form with your eyes open, then practice it at home for about 15 minutes, closing your eyes for one movement at first and adding one more each week. You stand within arm's reach of a wall or sturdy chair and open your eyes whenever you feel unsteady. A teacher checks your progress every few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find nature or outdoor settings hard to reach, or who prefer an inward, private practice at home. It may also suit anyone who wants a gentle way to work on balance and body awareness.
modalities.cautions: Closing your eyes makes balancing harder, so always practice next to a wall or chair on a clear, non-slip floor, and skip the eyes-closed parts if you have a balance disorder, dizziness or a history of falls. Open your eyes at once if you feel disoriented or anxious.
modalities.tweet: Close your eyes and keep moving, slowly. Eyes Closed Indoors is a new concept: learn a five-movement form eyes open, then practice it at home eyes closed, one movement at a time, always within reach of a wall. For people who rarely get outdoors.

modalities.name: Moving With Pictures
modalities.tagline: A set movement form where each move is paired with an image.
modalities.whatItIs: Moving With Pictures is a new concept for a fixed movement form in which every movement is paired with a simple inner image, such as lifting water, parting tall grass or pushing a cloud. A teacher introduces each image, and the image shapes how the movement feels.
modalities.coreIdea: Sensory mindfulness rests on plain sensing and lets experience be; this moves toward imagination and deliberately shaping each movement. The inner picture gives each move a quality to aim for, such as heavy, light or flowing.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small class, or at home after a few lessons, you work through eight movements for about 25 minutes, holding each image in mind as you move: scooping water from a river, parting grass, lifting a lantern, pushing a cloud away. The teacher sometimes swaps an image to show how it changes the movement. Practice usually ends with a minute of standing still with no image at all.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find plain body awareness dull and engage more easily through imagination. It could also work for children, artists and anyone who thinks in pictures.
modalities.cautions: Imagery-rich meditative practice is usually gentle, but anyone with a history of psychosis, dissociation or another serious mental illness should get medical advice first and learn with an experienced teacher. Adapt any movement that strains your joints or balance.
modalities.tweet: Scoop water from a river, part tall grass, push a cloud away. Moving With Pictures is a new concept: a slow form where each movement comes with an image that shapes how it feels. For anyone who finds plain body awareness a bit dull.

modalities.name: The Unaccompanied Form
modalities.tagline: A slow form practiced in total silence, no music at all.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unaccompanied Form is an invented way of practicing a slow, fixed movement form in complete silence, with no background music, no counting aloud and no recordings. The only sounds are your breath, your feet and whatever the room or street offers.
modalities.coreIdea: Music shapes sound, emotion and expression; this goes toward silence, calm and a form that expresses nothing. Without music to set the mood or the pace, the breath has to set it.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn a short form from a teacher, then practice it alone for about 20 minutes a day in the quietest place you can find, keeping time only by your own breathing. If you catch yourself humming or hearing a tune in your head, you return to the sound of your breath. Once a month you can join a silent group session where nobody speaks from start to finish.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who always have music or audio on and want to find out what practice is like without it. It may also suit anyone who finds the music in classes distracting.
modalities.cautions: Silence can make some people more aware of worries or of ringing in the ears, so start with short sessions and stop if it becomes distressing. Adapt movements to your body, and keep up any treatment you already have.
modalities.tweet: Most movement classes come with soft music. This one comes with none. The Unaccompanied Form is a new idea: a slow form practiced in total silence, timed only by your breath. Twenty minutes a day for anyone who always has something playing.

modalities.name: One Stranger a Day
modalities.tagline: A short, real conversation with someone new, every single day.
modalities.whatItIs: One Stranger a Day is a new concept for a self-led habit of starting one short, real conversation with someone you do not know, every day, in ordinary places like a queue, a park bench or a market stall. There is no script and no goal beyond the exchange itself.
modalities.coreIdea: The Ideal Parent Figure Protocol builds imagined caring figures, slowly, with a therapist and a plan; this pushes socializing the other way, toward real, unknown faces met live, with no plan and no guide. The liveliness of an unscripted encounter is the point.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each day you look for a natural opening with someone new, such as a comment about their dog, the weather or the book they are reading, and see where it goes for a minute or two. You do not keep score or plan lines in advance, and if someone does not want to chat, you smile and move on. Some days it is a nod and a sentence, and some days it turns into a real conversation.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want more spontaneity and fresh contact in their lives, especially after a move, a breakup or a long stretch of isolation. It could also work for anyone who would like public places to feel friendlier.
modalities.cautions: Stick to public places, respect people who do not want to talk and trust your instincts about personal safety. If fear of strangers or social situations is intense, talk to a doctor or therapist first rather than pushing through alone.
modalities.tweet: Imagine one real conversation a day with someone you have never met: in a queue, on a bench, at a market stall. One Stranger a Day is a new idea for people who want more fresh, unscripted contact. No script, no score, just say hello.

modalities.name: Deliberately Mixed Company
modalities.tagline: Seek out regular time with people unlike yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Deliberately Mixed Company is an untested idea for making a habit of spending social time with people who differ from you in age, background, work or outlook. You join gatherings outside your usual circle, such as a community kitchen, a neighborhood meeting or an intergenerational club, and simply take part.
modalities.coreIdea: IFS gets to know many inner voices with a therapist, through personal history; this turns outward instead, toward many real and different people met in the present, with no guide. Variety in your actual company is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you go to one gathering where you will probably be the odd one out, such as a chess club in the park, a language exchange or a community garden day, and talk with at least two people you would not normally meet. You listen more than you explain and ask about their lives. Over time you return to the places where you felt welcome.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose social life has become narrow or repetitive, or who live mostly among people just like them. It may also suit anyone curious about other lives who wants to feel more at home in the wider community.
modalities.cautions: Choose groups that welcome newcomers and are respectful to everyone, and leave any setting that turns hostile or unsafe. If walking into unfamiliar groups brings intense anxiety, start with a friend or talk to a professional about it.
modalities.tweet: Most of us spend our time with people a lot like us. Deliberately Mixed Company is a new concept: once a week, join one gathering where you are the odd one out, a chess club, a language exchange, a community garden, and talk to two new people.

modalities.name: Aimless Afternoons
modalities.tagline: Unplanned time with friends, with no agenda and no review afterward.
modalities.whatItIs: Aimless Afternoons is a new concept for unplanned social time with a few friends: you meet with no plan, no goal and no list of things to talk about, and drift wherever the afternoon takes you. Afterward you do not analyze how it went.
modalities.coreIdea: CBT sets agendas, tests predictions and reviews progress; this is company with no structure, no self-monitoring and an accepting attitude. Letting time with people be purposeless is the purpose.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every couple of weeks you and two to five friends pick a meeting point and a rough start time, and that is all you plan. You might wander a market, sit in a café, walk to a viewpoint or go home early, with every decision made on the spot. You keep your phone in your pocket and skip the mental replay of what you said.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who over-plan their social lives or replay every conversation afterward, and who want company that asks nothing of them. It could also work for busy friends whose meetups have turned into scheduled tasks.
modalities.cautions: Spend unstructured time with people you feel safe with, and step back from company that leaves you feeling worse. If social worries or low mood persist despite good company, talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: No plan, no goal, no replaying it afterward. Aimless Afternoons is a new idea: meet a few friends at a spot and a rough time, then drift wherever the afternoon goes, a market, a café, a walk, home early. For people who over-plan everything.

modalities.name: The Yes Month
modalities.tagline: For one month, say yes to every safe, reasonable invitation.
modalities.whatItIs: The Yes Month is a proposed month-long personal experiment: you say yes to every safe, reasonable social invitation that comes your way, from coffee after a meeting to a neighbor's barbecue. It needs no therapist and no plan, only a willingness to show up.
modalities.coreIdea: ACT works through metaphors and planned steps with a therapist; the opposite here is plain, unguided action: when people invite you, you go. Saying yes before hesitation has time to talk you out of it is the whole idea.
