modalities.whatYouDo: For thirty days you accept invitations by default, unless something is unsafe, unaffordable or clashes with a real commitment, and you go even when you would normally make an excuse. You can also say yes to small openings, such as joining colleagues for lunch or staying for a chat after a class. At the end of the month you decide which new connections you want to keep.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to decline invitations out of habit, low energy or nerves and suspect they are missing out. It may also suit newcomers to a town, job or school who want to build connections quickly.
modalities.cautions: Yes never covers anything unsafe, unaffordable or against your values, and you can still rest when you need to and turn down alcohol or anything else you do not want. If invitations feel frightening rather than awkward, or low mood makes everything hard, talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: What if you said yes to every safe, reasonable invitation for a month? The Yes Month is a new concept for people who habitually make excuses: coffee, lunch, a neighbor's barbecue, the chat after class. At the end, keep the connections you like.

modalities.name: Small Talk Rounds
modalities.tagline: Light, friendly chats with the familiar faces of your week.
modalities.whatItIs: Small Talk Rounds is a new concept for deliberately keeping up light, friendly chats with the familiar faces you pass in a week: the barista, the bus driver, the neighbor, the person at the next desk. Nothing deep is meant to happen; the point is warm, easy contact that repeats.
modalities.coreIdea: Coherence Therapy digs for the hidden emotional truths behind a problem; this keeps exchanges deliberately light and present-tense, with no digging at all. Many small, shallow contacts are valued in their own right.
modalities.whatYouDo: As you go about your week, you make a point of greeting the same people by name, asking one easy question, such as how their weekend was, and remembering the answer next time. Chats last a minute or two and stay on light topics like the weather, sport, pets or local news. Over the weeks these faces become a familiar web of people who know you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel invisible in their daily routine, or whose close relationships are few, and who would like more everyday warmth. It may also suit anyone who finds deep conversations draining but still wants contact.
modalities.cautions: Keep it light and respectful, and take the hint if someone is busy or not in the mood. Small talk is no replacement for close support, so if you feel persistently lonely or low, talk to someone you trust or to a professional.
modalities.tweet: The barista, the bus driver and the neighbor are part of your social life too. Small Talk Rounds is a new idea: a minute of light, friendly chat with the familiar faces of your week, remembering one thing each time. Nothing deep required.

modalities.name: Evening Call Circuit
modalities.tagline: Several voice calls in a row: just talk, no video, no screens.
modalities.whatItIs: Evening Call Circuit is an invented practice for a regular round of voice calls with several different people, one after another, made from the sofa. It is pure conversation: no video, no shared activity, nothing but voices.
modalities.coreIdea: TRE is physical, silent and done alone; this pushes socializing to the other extreme, with words only, many people and no body work at all. Talking is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three or four evenings a week you call two or three people in a row, such as a sibling, an old friend and someone you have lost touch with, for 10 to 20 minutes each. There is no agenda: you catch up, laugh and swap news, and you let calls run long or end early as they naturally do. If someone does not pick up, you leave a short, friendly message and move on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose friends and family are spread out, or who cannot easily get out in the evenings, and who want more regular contact. It might also appeal to anyone who finds voice calls more relaxed than video or meeting in person.
modalities.cautions: Keep calling the people who leave you feeling better rather than worse, and do not let calls crowd out sleep. If you find yourself calling to escape persistent low mood or loneliness, mention it to a doctor or therapist as well.
modalities.tweet: Remember long phone calls? Evening Call Circuit is a new concept: a few evenings a week, call two or three people in a row, a sibling, an old friend, someone you have lost touch with. Just voices, no video, no agenda. For far-flung friendships. 📞

modalities.name: Who's In Tonight
modalities.tagline: Propose a same-day plan to a group and go with whoever comes.
modalities.whatItIs: Who's In Tonight is a new concept for a habit of making spontaneous, same-day plans: you send a quick message to a group of friends proposing something for that evening and go with whoever says yes. It favors acting on the impulse to connect over waiting for the perfect moment.
modalities.coreIdea: Focusing waits slowly and quietly for something to form inside; this goes toward quick, outward, energetic action with other people. The lively, unplanned plan is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a week, when you notice you would like company, you message a group chat with a simple, concrete offer, such as a quiz night, a walk to the river or noodles at seven. Whoever replies joins you, and if nobody does, you go alone or try again another day without taking it personally. You keep the offers cheap and easy to say yes to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who wait for others to invite them and end up spending more evenings alone than they want. It could also work for friend groups that only meet when someone organizes weeks ahead.
modalities.cautions: Silence in reply is normal and not a rejection, and if it stings badly or often, that is worth talking through with someone you trust or a professional. Keep plans safe and affordable, and make alcohol optional rather than the point.
modalities.tweet: Ever wait all week for someone to invite you? Who's In Tonight is a new idea: message a group with one easy same-day plan, noodles at seven, a walk, a quiz, and go with whoever says yes. For people who want more spontaneous company.

modalities.name: Borrowed Sugar Habit
modalities.tagline: Ask neighbors and friends for small favors, and offer them back.
modalities.whatItIs: Borrowed Sugar Habit is an untested idea for deliberately weaving your social ties through small favors: asking a neighbor to lend you a ladder, offering to water someone's plants, swapping a lift for a home-cooked meal. Each favor creates a reason to talk again.
modalities.coreIdea: Aletheia Coaching slows down to let inner experience unfold; this goes toward brisk, practical action that changes your social world, done without any coach. Small acts of asking and giving become the threads of connection.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you ask one small, easy favor of someone nearby and offer one, such as borrowing a tool, sharing extra vegetables or carrying a parcel up the stairs. You return borrowed things promptly with a little thank-you, which often turns into a short chat. Over a few months you keep a rough sense of who helps whom and look for ways to even it out.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are reluctant to ask for help and have few ties in their street, building or workplace. It may also suit those who have just moved and want to become part of a neighborhood.
modalities.cautions: Keep favors small, easy to decline and evenly balanced over time, and never ask for anything that would put someone at risk or out of pocket. If asking for help feels impossible, that may be worth exploring with a therapist.
modalities.tweet: Asking a neighbor for a cup of sugar used to be normal. Borrowed Sugar Habit is a new concept: each week, ask one small favor and offer one, a ladder, a lift, some extra vegetables, then return things with a thank-you. For people new to a neighborhood.

modalities.name: Be the Convener
modalities.tagline: Start and host a small regular gathering yourself.
modalities.whatItIs: Be the Convener is a new concept for taking charge of your social life by starting and hosting a small, regular gathering: a monthly dinner, a walking group, a book swap or a games night. Instead of waiting to be included, you create the occasion and invite people in.
modalities.coreIdea: Do Nothing meditation sets out to change nothing; this is the reverse, with initiative, a light structure and active change in who you see and how often. Being the one who brings people together is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a simple format you would enjoy, set a fixed day, such as the first Friday of each month, and invite five to ten people, asking each to bring someone new once in a while. You handle the small jobs: reminders, a place to meet and a welcome at the door. After three or four gatherings you adjust the format based on who keeps coming and why.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel left out or tired of waiting for invitations, and who like having a project. It might also appeal to those who are good at organizing but rarely use that skill for friendship.
modalities.cautions: Hosting can become a burden, so keep the format cheap and simple, share the tasks and take a break when you need one. Turnout will vary, which says little about you, and if hosting brings intense worry, talk it over with someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: If nobody organizes it, it does not happen. Be the Convener is a new concept: pick a simple format, a monthly dinner, a walking group, a book swap, set a fixed day and invite five to ten people. For people with organizing energy to spare.

modalities.name: Tell Them Today
modalities.tagline: Say your appreciation out loud, face to face, the same day.
modalities.whatItIs: Tell Them Today is a proposed habit: when you feel appreciation, admiration or affection for someone, you tell them out loud, in person, that day. It turns kind thoughts into real, spoken moments with real people.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta cultivates goodwill silently, alone and toward people held in mind; this turns it into spoken words to real faces, with no set phrases. Saying it directly, while the feeling is fresh, is the whole practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Whenever you notice a warm thought about someone, such as a colleague who handled a meeting well or a friend whose humor made your week, you tell them that day in a sentence or two. You keep it simple and specific, for example that their help on Tuesday made a real difference. Some days that means three people, and some days none.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel warmly toward others but rarely say so, and who would like their relationships to feel closer. It may also appeal to anyone who practices loving-kindness meditation and wants to take it off the cushion.
modalities.cautions: Keep it honest and suited to the relationship, especially at work, and do not expect anything in return. Some people find compliments awkward, so a light touch works better than a speech.
modalities.tweet: Thought something kind about someone today and kept it to yourself? Tell Them Today is a new idea: when appreciation shows up, say it out loud, face to face, that same day, in a sentence or two. For people who feel warmly but rarely say so.

modalities.name: The Talking Weekend
modalities.tagline: The opposite of a silent retreat: a weekend of nonstop conversation.
modalities.whatItIs: The Talking Weekend is a new concept for a self-organized weekend away with a group of friends where conversation is the whole point: long meals, late nights and endless talk, with no screens and no schedule. It is the deliberate opposite of a silent retreat.
modalities.coreIdea: Vipassana turns attention inward, alone and without speaking, often on silent retreats; this takes socializing the opposite way, toward lively, wordy, shared time. Plenty of unhurried talk among friends is the core of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight friends rent a cabin or borrow a house for two nights, agree to put phones away and arrive with nothing planned except meals. You cook, eat and talk for hours, about memories, ideas, plans and nonsense, letting conversations split into pairs and come back together. On the last morning each person names one conversation they will remember.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose friendships have shrunk to quick messages and short catch-ups and who want to reconnect properly. It could also interest anyone who has tried silent retreats and is curious about the opposite.
modalities.cautions: A weekend of nonstop company can be tiring, so anyone should feel free to slip away for quiet time, and alcohol stays optional. Choose people you trust, and if old conflicts are likely to flare, agree in advance how to step back.
modalities.tweet: Silent retreats are a thing. What about the opposite? The Talking Weekend is a new concept: four to eight friends, one cabin, two nights, phones away, nothing planned but meals and hours of conversation. For friendships that have shrunk to texting.

modalities.name: Busy Hands, Easy Talk
modalities.tagline: Quiet hand tasks side by side, with slow, easy talk.
modalities.whatItIs: Busy Hands, Easy Talk is an untested idea for calm, low-key gatherings where everyone brings a quiet hand task, such as knitting, mending, sketching, a jigsaw or a bowl of beans to shell, and works on it alongside the others. Talk drifts in and out at an easy pace, and long silences are part of it.
modalities.coreIdea: HIIT is fast, hard and tightly timed; this is socializing slowed right down, with stillness, calm and no structure at all. Because hands and eyes have something gentle to do, nobody has to keep the conversation going.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week, four to ten people meet for about two hours at a kitchen table, a library room or a corner of a café, each with their own task and a cup of tea. You chat, show each other what you are making, ask for a hand or simply work in companionable quiet. There is no teacher, no project to finish and no need to be good at anything.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find face-to-face conversation tiring or busy social events exhausting but still want regular, easy company, including older adults and anyone recovering from burnout. It could also suit anyone whose hobby is usually done alone.
modalities.cautions: It is gentle by design, but loneliness or low mood that persists despite good company is worth raising with a doctor or therapist. Keep sharp tools safe around children, and choose a space that is easy to reach for people with limited mobility.
modalities.tweet: Knitting, mending, sketching, a jigsaw: bring any quiet hand task. Busy Hands, Easy Talk is a new idea for weekly gatherings where everyone works side by side and talk drifts in and out. For people who find face-to-face chat tiring. 🧶

modalities.name: Theme Jar Evenings
modalities.tagline: Friends trade true stories from their lives, with no winners.
modalities.whatItIs: Theme Jar Evenings is a new concept for relaxed evenings where a group of friends or neighbors take turns telling true stories from their lives, prompted by a theme drawn from a jar, such as a lucky escape or a first job. There are no teams, no scores and no winners, just stories and listening.
modalities.coreIdea: Team sport is physical, competitive and fast; this keeps the company but drops the contest, so people sit still, take turns and share without competing. Stories become the way people get to know each other.
modalities.whatYouDo: Six to twelve people meet in a living room or a café back room for about two hours, and someone draws a theme from a jar. Anyone who wants to tells a five-minute true story, the others listen without interrupting, and the talk afterward flows freely. Telling is always optional, and listening is a full part of the evening.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to know their friends or neighbors more deeply without the pressure of competitive or physical activities. It might also appeal to those who love stories but feel shy about small talk.
modalities.cautions: Some stories touch painful memories, so tellers choose what to share, listeners respond kindly and nobody should feel pressed to tell anything. If a story stirs up something heavy that lingers, talk to someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: An untested idea: Theme Jar Evenings. Six to twelve people, one theme pulled from a jar, such as a lucky escape or a first job, and five-minute true stories from anyone who wants to tell one. No teams, no scores, just stories and listening.

modalities.name: Open Door Evenings
modalities.tagline: One fixed evening a week when your door is open to friends.
modalities.whatItIs: Open Door Evenings is a proposed practice of keeping one fixed evening a week when friends and neighbors know they can drop by without asking. You stay home, put the kettle on and let whoever comes, come.
modalities.coreIdea: Endurance training means going out and covering distance under your own power; this does the reverse, staying put and letting company come to you. A standing open invitation, with almost no structure, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: You pick an evening, such as every Wednesday from seven to ten, and tell a circle of friends and neighbors that the door is open, with tea and something simple to eat. Some weeks five people come and some weeks one or none, and you carry on with your evening either way. Guests can bring a friend, help with the washing up or just sit and talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who would like more company but find organizing events tiring, and those who enjoy hosting in a relaxed way. It may also suit families or flatmates who want their home to be a small social hub.
modalities.cautions: Share the open invitation only with people you trust, keep it simple and cheap, and feel free to cancel when you need a quiet week. Turnout will vary, and if quiet evenings feel crushing, that is worth talking through with someone.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Open Door Evenings. One fixed night a week, your friends and neighbors know the kettle is on and the door is open. Some weeks five people drop in, some weeks nobody. For anyone who wants company without organizing anything.

modalities.name: Advice-Free Gatherings
modalities.tagline: Friends meet to listen to each other, with one rule: no advice.
modalities.whatItIs: Advice-Free Gatherings is a new concept for regular meetups of friends with one simple rule: nobody gives advice or tries to solve anyone else's problems. You talk about what is going on in your lives, and the others listen, ask questions and keep you company.
modalities.coreIdea: Strength training is about effort, progress and pushing to improve; this goes toward accepting each other as you are, with no improvement plans. Being heard without being managed is the heart of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight friends meet every couple of weeks over food or coffee for a couple of hours. When someone shares a struggle, the others respond with curiosity rather than suggestions, for example by asking what it has been like, and anyone can call 'advice alert' with a smile if the rule slips. If someone actually wants advice, they ask for it outright.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of getting unasked-for solutions from well-meaning friends, or who catch themselves giving advice instead of listening. It could also work for any friend group that wants to feel more supportive.
modalities.cautions: Listening is no substitute for professional help, so if someone shares something serious, such as thoughts of self-harm, the rule gives way and the group helps them get support. Keep the group small and every topic voluntary.
modalities.tweet: One rule: no advice. Advice-Free Gatherings is a new concept: four to eight friends meet every couple of weeks, share what is going on, and the others just listen and ask questions. For people tired of unasked-for solutions.

modalities.name: Seat Swap Suppers
modalities.tagline: A lively shared supper at one long table, strangers welcome.
modalities.whatItIs: Seat Swap Suppers is an invented format for lively, self-organized community meals where neighbors and strangers share one long table, talk and swap seats before dessert. There is no host on a stage, no program and no professional: just food, noise and conversation.
modalities.coreIdea: Animal-assisted therapy is calm, guided and often wordless; this pushes socializing the other way, to loud, chatty, unguided human company with nothing in between people. The long table puts everyone shoulder to shoulder with someone new.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a month a few volunteers borrow a hall, a courtyard or a closed-off street, push tables into one long line and invite anyone to bring a dish to share. You sit wherever there is space, introduce yourself to the people beside and across from you, and stay as long as you like, usually two or three hours. Seats change before dessert so everyone meets someone new.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a big, warm dose of human company and a way to meet people in their area. It may also suit anyone who finds one-to-one meetups intense but enjoys the buzz of a crowd.
modalities.cautions: Label dishes for common allergens, and keep the event open, alcohol optional and safe for everyone, including children and older guests. Noisy crowds can be overwhelming, so a quiet corner or an early exit should always be fine.
modalities.tweet: One long table, a dish each, neighbors and strangers side by side. Seat Swap Suppers is a new idea for monthly community meals with no program, just food, lively talk and a change of seats before dessert. For people who want to meet their area. 🍲

modalities.name: Into the Crowd
modalities.tagline: Seek out busy, buzzing public gatherings and join in.
modalities.whatItIs: Into the Crowd is a new concept for regularly joining lively public gatherings, such as street festivals, markets, fan zones and local celebrations, and mixing with the people there. The aim is to soak up the buzz of a crowd and chat with whoever is beside you.
modalities.coreIdea: Qigong is quiet, slow, mostly solitary and set in its form; this goes toward noise, spontaneity and the energy of many people at once. Shared excitement in a crowd is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once or twice a month you check local listings and go to one busy public event, alone or with a friend, for an hour or two. You join in where you can, such as clapping along, cheering, asking a stallholder about their food or chatting to the people next to you. You leave whenever you have had enough.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel flat, isolated or stuck at home and want a jolt of collective energy. It might also appeal to those who like being among people without the pressure of one-to-one conversation.
modalities.cautions: Crowds can be overwhelming or unsafe, so know your exits, drink water, keep alcohol moderate or skip it, and leave if things feel tense. If crowds bring on panic, start with smaller events and talk to a professional.
modalities.tweet: Feeling flat? Try a crowd. Into the Crowd is a new concept: once or twice a month, go to one buzzing public event, a street festival, a market, a fan zone, and join in by cheering, chatting or clapping along. Leave whenever you have had enough.

modalities.name: Board Game Regulars
modalities.tagline: A standing weekly game night at the same table, with familiar faces.
modalities.whatItIs: Board Game Regulars is an untested idea for becoming a regular at a weekly indoor game night, in a café, a library or someone's home, with the same core group. The games give everyone a shared focus, a little friendly competition and plenty of excuses to talk.
modalities.coreIdea: Nature walks are open, outdoors and full of the senses; this brings socializing indoors, around a table, with light rules and lively interaction. The game's structure carries the social side for people who find open-ended chat hard.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every week at the same time you join a table of three to six people for two or three hours of board or card games, from quick party games to slower strategy games. Between rounds you chat, teach each other new games and swap news. Over time you get to know the regulars and they get to know you.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find unstructured socializing awkward and prefer having something to do together. It may also suit anyone who enjoys a bit of competition and wants a reliable weekly fixture.
modalities.cautions: Keep the mood friendly, choose games where losing is easy to laugh off, and step away from groups that turn hostile. Watch the cost of café fees or buying games, and keep alcohol optional.
modalities.tweet: Some of us talk best with dice in hand. 🎲 Board Game Regulars is a new idea: the same weekly game night, same table, same core group, at a café, a library or someone's home. For people who find open-ended chat awkward.

modalities.name: Friendly Argument Club
modalities.tagline: Lively, good-humored debate about ideas, among friends who disagree.
modalities.whatItIs: Friendly Argument Club is a new concept for regular evenings where friends gather to argue, in good humor, about ideas, books, films or big questions. The aim is lively exchange and changing minds, your own included, rather than calm agreement.
modalities.coreIdea: Sensory mindfulness is quiet, solitary and rooted in the senses; this goes toward ideas, enthusiastic voices and active attempts to persuade. Disagreeing well, together, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to ten people meet every couple of weeks in a home or a pub back room, someone brings a question, such as whether cities should ban cars, and the group argues it out for an hour or two. Anyone can switch sides partway through, and the evening ends with everyone saying what, if anything, moved them. Insults are off limits, and laughing at a good point from the other side is encouraged.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love ideas, find polite small talk dull and want friends who will push back. It could also work for anyone who wants to practice disagreeing without falling out.
modalities.cautions: Avoid topics that touch someone's identity or recent pain unless everyone agrees to them, and stop if an argument turns personal or hostile. If conflict makes you very anxious, start as a listener.
modalities.tweet: Bored of polite small talk? Friendly Argument Club is a new concept: five to ten friends, one big question, an hour or two of good-humored debate, and anyone can switch sides. It ends with everyone saying what changed their mind.

modalities.name: Phones in the Basket
modalities.tagline: Gatherings with phones in a basket and no background music.
modalities.whatItIs: Phones in the Basket is a proposed practice for get-togethers where everyone drops their phone in a basket at the door and the music stays off, so nothing competes with the conversation. You hear each other properly, and attention stays on the faces in the room.
modalities.coreIdea: Music fills a room with sound and mood. This strips the background away and leaves plain, undistracted conversation with the people actually present.
modalities.whatYouDo: Whenever you host friends, for dinner, drinks or a lazy afternoon, you put a basket by the door, ask guests to leave their phones in it and keep the music off. The evening is just talk, food and whatever the group decides to do, with no screens and no soundtrack. Anyone can step out to check their phone if they need to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice that gatherings keep getting interrupted by screens or drowned out by music and want fuller conversations. It may also suit anyone with hearing difficulties, for whom background noise makes talk hard to follow.
modalities.cautions: Keep a way to be reached in emergencies, such as leaving ringers on in the basket, and never pressure someone who needs their phone for health, care or work reasons. A quiet room can feel awkward at first, so a game or a shared task can help break the ice.
modalities.tweet: No phones, no playlist, just the people in the room. Phones in the Basket is a new idea for get-togethers: phones go in a basket at the door, music stays off, and the conversation gets your full attention. For anyone tired of half-listening.
